findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. This works well.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page says why a study of another project is on Athena's homepage: it is a demonstration. Without this, the firstmate content would confuse a newcomer.
findings.source: Header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project"

findings.text: Athena gets three sentences. Nearly everything else is a detailed state machine for a project the newcomer probably has never heard of. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past dense firstmate detail, or skip straight to the Next steps link.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions", "Claims and sources"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: requirements, clone, install, then a first command to try. A newcomer knows exactly what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: "Predictions" is not explained anywhere on the page, so the newcomer cannot tell what Athena will show them before it runs.
findings.source: Next steps: "It shows how it read the request and its predictions; press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: This link speaks to the owner as "your". A newcomer cannot tell whether it is meant for them or what the proposals are.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The page promises cost tracking and a reviewer's verdict, but never shows one. It shows a study instead, so the main thing a newcomer would want to see is only described.
findings.source: Header lede: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: The state list gives only a name, a tag and claim ids. Definitions are in the lead-in paragraph and the Glossary, so a reader has to jump around to understand each state.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "ready waiting"

findings.text: The page openly admits gaps and limits (also in "Limits of this study"). That supports the claim that it is traceable, but it adds more for a newcomer to take in.
findings.source: Glossary: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."
